title: Forensic Audit (Fraud Investigation)
stem: Forensic Audit (Fraud Investigation) A scheduled commercial bank sanctioned working capital limits to five unrelated companies over a period of eight months. During RBI inspection, the following facts emerged: • All borrowers had submitted invoices issued by different suppliers. • GSTIN verification showed that three suppliers did not exist. • Funds were transferred to multiple accounts and withdrawn within 48 hours. • Stock statements submitted every month showed exactly identical quantities despite different industries. • Concurrent audit had not reported any irregularity. The Board appoints a forensic auditor. Which investigative approach would most effectively establish whether a coordinated lending fraud has occurred?
opts: Compare interest income earned from each account with industry averages and quantify revenue leakage.
Perform end-use verification by tracing fund movement, validating digital evidence, confirming supplier existence and reconstructing the transaction trail before identifying responsible individuals.
Recalculate drawing power from stock statements and revise provisioning as per IRAC norms.
Review branch profitability, employee performance ratings and internal audit observations to determine whether sanction limits exceeded delegated authority.
ex: A coordinated lending fraud across unrelated borrowers can only be established by tracing the actual flow of funds, verifying whether suppliers genuinely exist, examining digital evidence and reconstructing the transaction trail — not by relying on ratio comparisons or profitability reviews, which would not reveal fabricated documentation or circular fund movement.

title: Earnings Per Share (Corporate Action & Dilution)
stem: Earnings Per Share (Corporate Action & Dilution) ABC Technologies Ltd. reported the following for FY 2025--26: • Profit after Tax: ₹48 crore • Equity Shares outstanding throughout the year: 2 crore shares • 12% Convertible Debentures of ₹20 crore were converted into equity on 1 October 2025. • Annual post-tax interest attributable to these debentures is ₹1.2 crore. • Conversion results in issue of 20 lakh additional equity shares. While reviewing the financial statements, the CFO states: "Basic EPS and Diluted EPS will remain identical because the conversion happened during the year." How should the auditor evaluate this statement?
opts: Correct, because convertible securities issued during the year are ignored for EPS computation.
Incorrect, because diluted EPS requires adjusting both earnings and weighted average number of shares for the dilutive effect of potential equity shares.
Correct, because interest savings are considered only after actual conversion at year-end.
Incorrect, because only the denominator changes while the numerator always remains unchanged under diluted EPS.
ex: Diluted EPS must reflect the dilutive effect of potential equity shares outstanding during the year — both the weighted average number of shares (adjusted for the period the debentures were outstanding as debt) and the earnings (added back with post-tax interest saved) need adjustment. Basic and Diluted EPS will therefore differ even though conversion happened during the year.

title: Multiple Costing (Costing Decision)
stem: Multiple Costing (Costing Decision) Omega Engineering manufactures industrial air-conditioning systems. Production involves: • Compressors manufactured through continuous processing. • Copper coils produced in batches. • Final installation and commissioning performed separately for every customer. • Annual Maintenance Contracts (AMC) are monitored customer-wise. The Finance Director proposes introducing one uniform costing method across all activities to simplify reporting. The Cost Accountant objects. Which of the following provides the strongest professional justification for the objection?
opts: Since every product eventually becomes part of one final system, Process Costing alone provides the most accurate product cost.
Different stages consume resources in fundamentally different ways; therefore, combining Process Costing, Batch Costing and Job Costing improves cost measurement and managerial decision-making.
Marginal Costing eliminates the need for product costing and therefore should replace all traditional costing systems.
Uniform Costing is prohibited under Cost Accounting Standards whenever installation services are involved.
ex: A single company can validly use different costing methods for different stages of production — Process Costing for continuous compressor manufacture, Batch Costing for coils produced in batches, and Job/Contract Costing for customer-specific installation — because costing method should match the nature of each activity, not be forced into one uniform system.

title: Error of Omission (Trial Balance & Financial Statements)
stem: Error of Omission (Trial Balance & Financial Statements) While conducting a peer review, the auditor discovers the following: • Goods costing ₹3,20,000 were sold on credit for ₹4,80,000. • The entire transaction was omitted from the Sales Day Book. • Inventory records were updated correctly after dispatch. • Customer confirmation includes the receivable. • No other accounting errors exist. Before rectification, which statement best explains the effect on the financial statements?
opts: Trial Balance will disagree because Debtors are understated.
Gross Profit and Trade Receivables are understated, while the Trial Balance may still agree.
Closing Stock will be overstated by ₹4,80,000.
Net Profit remains unaffected because both sales and cost are omitted.
ex: Since a sale was completely omitted from the books, both sales revenue and the corresponding debtor were understated, which understates Gross Profit and Trade Receivables. Because the entry was omitted entirely (not entered incorrectly on one side), both the debit and credit simply do not appear, so the Trial Balance still agrees despite the error.

title: Cumulative Preference Shares
stem: Cumulative Preference Shares Delta Infrastructure Ltd. has 10% Cumulative Preference Share Capital of ₹15 crore. Because of heavy losses, the company could not declare dividends during FY 2023--24 and FY 2024--25. In FY 2025--26, after-tax profits are sufficient to declare dividends. During the Board Meeting, the following opinions are expressed: 1. Preference shareholders automatically become equity shareholders after two years of unpaid dividend. 2. Dividend arrears on cumulative preference shares must ordinarily be cleared before any dividend is declared on equity shares. 3. Arrears of cumulative preference dividend represent accumulated contractual preference rights rather than current year's dividend alone. 4. Non-payment of cumulative dividend reduces the paid-up preference share capital. Which combination is correct?
opts: Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1, 2 and 4 only
Statements 2, 3 and 4 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
ex: Arrears of cumulative preference dividend accumulate as a contractual right (Statement 3) and must ordinarily be cleared before any dividend can be paid to equity shareholders (Statement 2). Non-payment does not convert preference shareholders into equity shareholders, nor does it reduce paid-up preference capital, so Statements 1 and 4 are incorrect.

title: Rights Issue (Corporate Finance & Shareholder Wealth)
stem: Rights Issue (Corporate Finance & Shareholder Wealth) A listed company announces a Rights Issue of 1 share for every 4 shares held at ₹180 per share. The current market price is ₹260. Mr. Arjun owns 8,000 shares, but due to temporary liquidity constraints, he neither subscribes to the rights issue nor renounces his entitlement. After completion of the issue, which consequence is most likely?
opts: His ownership percentage may decline because he neither exercised nor monetized his valuable entitlement.
His existing shares become invalid until rights are exercised.
He loses all voting rights attached to existing shares.
His investment value necessarily increases because market price always rises after rights issues.
ex: A rights issue offers existing shareholders new shares below market price; a shareholder who neither subscribes nor sells (renounces) the entitlement suffers economic dilution because their percentage ownership falls while they gain nothing for the value of the right they let lapse.

title: Bond Valuation (Integrated Numerical)
stem: Bond Valuation (Integrated Numerical) An investor is evaluating two bonds issued by the same company. Bond A • Face Value = ₹1,000 • Coupon = 8% • Maturity = 4 years Bond B • Face Value = ₹1,000 • Coupon = 12% • Maturity = 4 years The required market yield suddenly increases from 8% to 11% because of rising interest rates. Which statement best reflects the combined effect on valuation?
opts: Both bonds will continue to trade at par because coupon rates remain unchanged.
Bond A will experience a larger percentage decline in price than Bond B because its coupon is lower than the prevailing market yield.
Bond B will appreciate because investors prefer higher coupon bonds during rising interest-rate cycles.
Both bonds will decline by exactly the same percentage because maturity is identical.
ex: A bond's price sensitivity to interest rate changes is inversely related to its coupon rate for a given maturity — lower-coupon bonds have relatively more of their value tied up in the distant redemption payment, making them more sensitive to yield changes, so Bond A (lower coupon) falls by a greater percentage than a higher-coupon bond of the same maturity.

title: Trade Bill Representing No Sale (Accommodation Bill)
stem: Trade Bill Representing No Sale (Accommodation Bill) Three companies controlled by the same promoter face liquidity pressure before the financial year-end. During inspection, the Credit Officer argues that since the bill is legally accepted, it represents a genuine trade transaction. Which conclusion is technically correct?
opts: The bill is valid because legal acceptance alone establishes a genuine commercial transaction.

ex: An accommodation bill is drawn and accepted without any underlying sale of goods, purely to raise finance — it is legally enforceable as a negotiable instrument, but because there is no genuine trade transaction backing it, it carries higher credit risk for the bank that discounts it.

title: Golden Rule of Real Accounts
stem: Golden Rule of Real Accounts The following transactions occurred during April: 1. Purchased machinery by issuing a cheque. 2. Paid installation charges in cash. 3. Purchased spare parts for immediate repairs. 4. Exchanged an old machine for a new one by paying the balance through bank. A trainee accountant proposes the following conclusion: *"Every transaction involving machinery should always be debited to Machinery Account because machinery is a Real Account."* The Chief Accountant disagrees. Which explanation is technically correct?
opts: Every expenditure relating to machinery must be capitalised irrespective of its nature.
Only expenditure resulting in acquisition or enhancement of future economic benefits should be capitalised; routine repairs should be charged to revenue even though they relate to machinery.
Installation charges are always indirect expenses.
The Golden Rule applies only to cash transactions.
ex: Under the Golden Rule for Real Accounts (Debit what comes in, Credit what goes out), only expenditure that brings a future economic benefit into the business — i.e., that enhances or extends the asset's capacity or life — should be capitalised. Routine repairs that merely restore existing performance are revenue expenditure and must be charged to the Statement of Profit and Loss.

title: Limited Liability Partnership (LLP)
stem: Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) Five professionals intend to start a consulting practice. They want: • Limited liability. • Separate legal identity. • Perpetual succession. • Ability to own assets in the firm's name. One partner argues that a traditional partnership already provides all these benefits. Which statement is technically correct?
opts: Traditional partnerships and LLPs have identical legal characteristics.

ex: An LLP is a separate legal entity distinct from its partners, has perpetual succession (unaffected by changes in partners), and offers limited liability protection — features that distinguish it fundamentally from a traditional partnership firm, where partners have unlimited personal liability.

title: Forfeiture of Shares
stem: Forfeiture of Shares ABC Ltd. issued equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹2. Premium was payable on allotment. A shareholder paid only the application money and failed to pay both allotment and final call. The shares were subsequently forfeited. Which accounting treatment is appropriate?
opts: Securities Premium Account remains unaffected because premium becomes payable only on reissue.
Since the premium due on allotment was never received, Securities Premium Account should be debited while recording forfeiture.
Share Capital should be debited only for the amount actually received.
Entire forfeited amount should immediately be transferred to Capital Reserve.
ex: Since the premium amount due at allotment was never actually received from the shareholder before forfeiture, the Securities Premium Account (which had been credited assuming the premium was receivable) must be reversed by debiting it at the time the shares are forfeited.

title: Accounting Standard 10 (Major Inspection Cost)
stem: Accounting Standard 10 (Major Inspection Cost) Nova Petrochem Ltd. owns a high-capacity turbine used in continuous production. As per statutory safety regulations, a major inspection must be carried out every five years before the turbine can continue operations. During FY 2025--26, the company incurred ₹2.80 crore on the inspection. No new component was installed, but without the inspection the turbine could not legally operate. The Accounts Manager proposes charging the entire expenditure to the Statement of Profit and Loss because "no new asset has been purchased." The Statutory Auditor disagrees. Which accounting treatment is most appropriate under AS 10?
opts: Charge the expenditure entirely to revenue because inspection does not increase production capacity.
Capitalise the inspection cost if the recognition criteria are satisfied, since it enables future economic benefits from continued use of the asset.
Transfer the expenditure to Deferred Revenue Expenditure.
Adjust the expenditure directly against General Reserve.
ex: Under AS 10, a major inspection cost can be capitalised as part of the asset's carrying amount if it meets the general recognition criteria (i.e., it enables continued use and future economic benefits will flow to the entity), rather than being expensed off merely because it does not directly enhance production capacity.

Which accounting treatment is most appropriate under AS 12?
opts: Recognise the subsidy immediately as Other Income because every Government grant is revenue in nature.

opts: Statements 1, 2 and 3 only

Statements 2 and 3 only
All four statements
ex: Yield to Maturity reflects both the coupon income and the gain/loss arising from the difference between purchase price and redemption value; a bond purchased below par (Bond X at ₹960) will have a YTM higher than its coupon, while one purchased above par (Bond Y at ₹1,050) will have a YTM lower than its coupon — matching Statements 1, 2 and 3, while Statement 4 is incorrect since coupon rate and YTM are equal only when a bond is purchased exactly at par.

stem: AS 10 -- Capital vs Revenue Expenditure Neptune Cements Ltd. purchased a kiln. ex: Under AS 10, expenditure that enhances the asset's future economic benefits — such as freight and installation on acquisition, or replacement of a major component that improves or extends the asset's working life — is capitalised, while routine maintenance that merely keeps the asset working as originally intended is charged to revenue.

title: Standard Costing (Variance Analysis)
stem: Standard Costing (Variance Analysis) A manufacturing company establishes standard material consumption for production. Actual purchase price is lower than standard price, but actual material consumption exceeds the standard quantity. The Production Manager concludes that overall material performance is favourable because the purchase price is lower. The Cost Controller disagrees. Which statement is correct?
opts: Material Price Variance alone determines efficiency.
A favourable Material Price Variance may be offset by an adverse Material Usage Variance.
Standard Costing ignores quantity consumed.
Material Usage Variance is relevant only when production is below budget.
ex: Material Price Variance (arising from a difference between standard and actual purchase price) and Material Usage Variance (arising from a difference between standard and actual quantity consumed) are independent variances; a favourable price variance (cheaper purchase) can easily be accompanied by an adverse usage variance (more material wasted), so total variance must be analysed by both components rather than price alone.

title: Change in Useful Life (Accounting Estimate)
stem: Change in Useful Life (Accounting Estimate) Atlas Engineering Ltd. revises the estimated useful life of a machine after obtaining a technical report indicating faster technological obsolescence. The Finance Executive proposes recalculating depreciation from the date of acquisition and restating previous financial statements. Which accounting treatment is correct?
opts: Apply the revised estimate prospectively because it represents a change in accounting estimate.
Restate previous financial statements.
Depreciation method cannot be revised.
Adjust the difference directly against retained earnings.
ex: A revision in an asset's useful life is a change in accounting estimate, not a change in accounting policy or a correction of an error; under AS 5, such changes are applied prospectively — spreading the remaining depreciable amount over the revised remaining useful life — without restating prior years' financial statements.

ex: Margin of Safety measures the excess of actual (or budgeted) sales over the break-even sales level, indicating how much sales can fall before the business starts incurring losses — it is a cushion/buffer concept in Cost-Volume- Profit analysis, unrelated to depreciation or impairment.

opts: Current Yield measures annual coupon income relative to market price, whereas Yield to Maturity also considers capital gain/loss and the time value of money.

Yield to Maturity ignores redemption value.
Current Yield applies only to Government Securities.
ex: Current Yield is simply the annual coupon (interest) payment divided by the bond's current market price, capturing only income return, whereas Yield to Maturity is a more complete measure that also factors in any capital gain or loss on redemption and the time value of money over the bond's remaining life, so the two figures generally differ except when a bond trades exactly at par.
